title: Who Wrote Lalita's Thousand Names
hookLine: the hymn's own story: goddesses of speech compose her names, and she hands them to everyone
carry: her names were given so anyone could call her

cards: The court is full. Gods, goddesses, sages and attendants are packed in before the throne of the goddess Lalita. Then the goddesses of speech step forward and begin to recite, name after name.

That's the scene the Brahmanda Purana gives for where the Lalita Sahasranama came from. The whole hymn is set inside a conversation: Hayagriva, a horse-headed form of Vishnu, teaching the sage Agastya.
And when Agastya hears the names, he's also told how they began, and what the goddess did when she heard them.

teach.h: LALITA CALLS THE GODDESSES OF SPEECH.
teach.b: Here's the story, in paraphrase, as the text tells it.

Lalita calls the goddesses of speech, the Vagdevis, Vashini and her companions, and asks them to compose a hymn of her secret names, so that her devotees might have a way to please her. They compose it.
Then one day, with the whole court gathered, the goddess signals to them, and the Vagdevis stand and recite the names they've made. The court is amazed.

teach.h: SHE TELLS EVERYONE TO RECITE THEM.
teach.b: And the goddess, pleased, tells everyone assembled to recite it: this hymn, made at her command, is the way to her favor. Notice who starts it. Not a poet trying to climb up to heaven.
The goddess herself asks for her names to be made, so her people would have a way to reach her.
That's a real thread in Hindu devotion: a divine name isn't a label people stick on God. Many teachers call it a door, and here God is the one who opens it.
It's why so many deities have a sahasranama, a thousand names, and why a family may offer one flower or one pinch of kumkum with each name.
Tradition keeps reverence around this hymn too; some teachers say it should be received from a teacher, not picked up casually. Both live side by side.
But the scene ends with the doors open. So when a grandmother sits down on a Friday and works through the names, she isn't trying to catch the goddess's attention.
In the hymn's own story, the goddess handed her the way in.

how: Some devotees learn the Lalita Sahasranama from a teacher and recite it daily or on Fridays; in a temple or home archana, a name is offered with each flower or pinch of kumkum, in the form 'om … namah.'

games.q: you're Lalita. the goddesses of speech have just recited the hymn of your names before your whole court, and everyone is amazed. what do you do?

tell everyone assembled to recite it.
games.why: pleased, she tells the whole court to recite it: the hymn made at her command becomes the way to her favor.

practice: Choose one name from the hymn that you've met this week, the one who gives grace, the one fond of devotion, the one without form, or simply the name Lalita, and say it once, quietly.

Let the silence after it be as long as the name, then say it again, unhurried. If you pray, you can offer the name back to the goddess each time; if you don't, notice what a single word does when it's given room.

wordCard.voice: The Lalita Sahasranama: Lalita's thousand names. In the text's own story, composed by the goddesses of speech at her command, and given to everyone in her court.

orig.note: Sanskrit vāgdevī: 'goddess of speech.' in the story, the vāgdevīs compose the hymn's names.
